item.content:encoded:
Reluctantly upvoted. It's well written and engaging, the twist genuinely surprised me and the well obscufated body horror is top notch.

It pretty strongly conflicts with my headcanon though. I don't like the idea that all of the Foundation's fictional technology are actually just repurposed anomalies that they don't truly understand (I disagree with SCP-3000 for the same reason.) I prefer SRAs as mundane but advanced technology because I like to think that a fantastically well funded organization of scientists who have studied the anomalous for decades would have actually learned something about them. I'm also not a fan of SRAs actually being invented by Prometheus and sold to the Foundation for the same reason. It makes the Foundation look incompetent.

Still though, like I said it's a great article and I enjoyed reading it. Good work.

A long-delayed reply - thanks for the nitpicks, seeprybyrun. I've fixed at least the majority of those, although I'm not 100% on exactly which of my commas are Oxford-style - I've kept a few which I think are necessary for ease of comprehension.

In terms of your question on British English idiom, that is entirely my fault and not an in-universe choice. I'm happy to consider changes if you point them out - my headcanon is that PL is primarily a US-based institution.

In terms of your last question - my understanding is that PL grant requests are internal only. That just seems to be how PL operates - budgetary allocations are referred to as grants.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I like this article as a proposal for the history of Scranton reality anchors. As mentioned above, it obfuscates what is being done to the reality benders ("recruitment" and "terms of employment" for "kidnapping" and "slavery" are my favorite euphemisms here), and that obfuscation enhances the horror of what is being done. George Orwell would be… proud? Disgusted?

However, I have some grammatical nitpicks that take me out of the story:

  • The Oxford comma is sometimes used, sometimes not. Either choice is fine, but it should be consistent throughout.
  • "US Dollars as at 1982" should probably be "US Dollars as of 1982."
  • "Initial design and testing of the devices is anticipated…" should be "are anticipated…"
  • "Information of the terms…" should probably be "Information about the terms…"

It is also curious that British English spelling and grammatical conventions are used but that currency is measured in USD. Is there an in-universe reason for this?

This also leads me to another question I have about the article: to whom is the grant request addressed? Is PL requesting a grant from an external agency (like a professor might request funding from the National Science Foundation in the U.S.), or is this proposal part of an internal process to obtain funding for a project within the Labs? (If the latter, the term "grant" seems an odd choice of terminology, though I suppose PL could have its own quirky jargon for such processes.)

No vote for now, but leaning towards +1.

item.content:encoded:
Interesting your thought about clinical tone. Changing this draft from SCP to PL format was an exercise in changing the tone - it retains a lot of the quasi-scientific language, but the PL format encourages the use of marketing-speak and corporate euphemisms. My personal favourite is "the terms of their employment has leaked to the market. As a result, future recruitment efforts are expected to be heavily contested…".

I know that PL isn't meant to be the "capitalism is evil" GOI, but I like the idea of their enthusiasm for the science leading them to take shortcuts on the ethics. This PL format article was definitely an influence on me in that respect.

item.content:encoded:
who is now maintaining (and recruiting) the ORIs?

Again, I like to think that this leaves open three answers to this question, all of which are rather unpleasant:

1) The Foundation knows exactly how SRAs work, and has taken over "employment" of the ORIs.

2) The provision of ORI-related services has been transitioned from PL to its external service providers, and the Foundation doesn't realise who is behind those front companies.

3) The eventual marketing materials for SRAs didn't reveal the existence of external services at all, and the Foundation hasn't realised yet that it is relying on a bunch of beryllium-bronze paperweights with no reality-maintaining effect.

That last option is probably the fate of the Nornirian cluster bombs that sirpudding refers to - that is (presuming that they work on similar principles to this proposal) the reality benders originally powering them have long-since died or are too far away, and thus the bombs are inactive.

item.content:encoded:
There's a few options there, but…

+ show block
– hide block

For the purposes of this article, I'd be willing to buy that the source of their power is their brains, but that wouldn't address things like differences in their strength of their abilities, aptitude with/control of said abilities, or differences in the abilities themselves.

This seems to be positing "Catch 1x Bixby, insert into machine" as if they're all more or less interchangeable, and the idea that there's a relatively non-limited supply of people out there with generic reality-bending powers at a standard level of power just isn't narratively interesting.

I'm pretty sure none of the reality benders in Foundation custody follow a perfectly identical pattern (i guess the witch is pretty similar to the superhero kid and that one guy who's a pile of organs, before he died anyway…), and people only tend to mention standard generic evil reality benders when they're giving somebody's tragic backstory.

As for other origins for powers… on the wiki we've got young deities, humans who seem to naturally emanate alternate theories of magic, extradimensional fae with a literal Hume-storing magic organ, and a man who may or may not be God, all of whom are probably classed as reality benders.

You've also got two children who are developing into Bixbys with different levels and types of power and control (One in a coma, one who should be), and two deceased ones (One whose powers came out with dementia, one who cursed themselves to be a pile of organs). None of them exactly alike.

item.content:encoded:
I liked this! I liked it a lot.

My only nitpick is how does PL avoid scarring of the brain, as happens very often in invasive brain-computer interfaces?1 I can't find any good sources on how long until brain scarring ruins the whole situation - I'd assume it depends on the specific equipment installed and the immune system/etc of the one with the brain shenanigans going on - but the efficiency of the ORI would deteriorate over time with potentially extremely varying times where they dip below an acceptable threshold.
It wouldnt be me if I didn't find some kind of scientific writing lacking some obscure detail

Footnotes
1. "Because they lie in the grey matter, invasive devices produce the highest quality signals of BCI devices but are prone to scar-tissue build-up, causing the signal to become weaker, or even non-existent, as the body reacts to a foreign object in the brain."

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Hmmmm….

This is a pretty vast improvement over the original post as an SCP article. I think it's a pretty solid exploration, and I was going to complain about your neurological description early on but you got more into detail later, so the science checks out.

You told this story very well, but I can't quite suspend my disbelief about the idea that there are a significant number of reality benders walking around with the same powers and casual mechanism. It just clashes hard with my ideas about the Foundation-verse, and I don't see the problem with heterogeneity addressed here. That's unfortunate, since I like just about everything else.

No vote for now, but I might flip up on reflection.

This is a re-write (in PL GoI-format) of a previous mainlist article - it has changed substantially (albeit not fundamentally) since its earlier incarnation.

Many thanks to the many people who looked this over and offered their thoughts:

  • sirpudding, who still doesn't believe in this type of SRA, but was always ready to share thoughts and lore about how an SRA should really work
  • Dr Reach, for an amazing interlude on Nornirian Cluster Bombs
  • dankaar, for coming up with a punchline to end this on
  • MrWrong and Scorpion451, for finding ways to de-power the anchors, and reminding me to *actually read* what SCP-2000 says, instead of making it up
  • A Random Day, for useful thoughts about worldbuilding

Apologies to those who I've forgotten to credit. Thanks ophite too for providing a reason to rush this prototype to market!
